name: op_add_remove_timer
description:
APP TIMERS: `CallbackInfo::add_timer` / `remove_timer`, i.e. the `CallbackChange::AddTimer` / `RemoveTimer` arms of `apply_user_change`. Those two arms were implemented in both hosts and reachable from NOTHING in the suite: a `CallbackChange::AddTimer` carries a Rust `TimerCallback` fn pointer, which a JSON scenario cannot supply, so the only timer any scenario could arm was the caret blink — and that goes through the separate `StartCursorBlinkTimer` arm. The `add_timer` / `remove_timer` debug ops close the gap by supplying the one thing JSON cannot (the callback) and pushing it through the same two `CallbackInfo` methods a real app calls; the canned callback rewrites the

's text to ' ' on every expiry, so a fired timer is visible as REAL PIXEL DAMAGE and not merely as a registry entry. BEAT 1 — register a 200 ms timer and tick 300 ms past its interval: the text changes and `assert_changed` sees non-empty damage AND differing pixels. BEAT 2 — tick again: it fires AGAIN. The appended run count is what makes that beat meaningful — `ChangeNodeText` correctly short-circuits a byte-identical write, so a constant-text timer would damage once and every later expiry would be indistinguishable from a dead timer. BEAT 3 — the beat that matters most: `remove_timer`, then two further 400 ms ticks must produce `FrameDamage::None`, and `assert_idle_stable` pins the pixels too. A `RemoveTimer` arm that silently did nothing would look EXACTLY like success up to this point, and the leaked timer would keep rewriting and repainting an idle window forever — the 'idle window never settles' class this suite exists to catch. Timer id 4242 is above USER_TIMER_ID_START (0x0100); the op refuses the reserved block by name, because registering there would overwrite an engine timer (caret blink / scroll momentum / tooltip / long press) instead of testing one. DOM mirrors e2e/bug-dom-mutation-no-damage.json so node id 10 is a stable text node. It deliberately does NOT use "Azul Mock Mono": every glyph in the mock fonts is the SAME filled rectangle (scripts/gen_mock_fonts.py — 'nothing about the SHAPE is meaningful'), so 'tick 1' and 'tick 2' would be pixel-identical under it and beat 2 could not tell a firing timer from a dead one. Measured, not assumed: the first version of this scenario used the mock font and beat 2 failed with 'damage was reported but NO pixel changed'.
